78:37.title: Silence Before the Lord of Mercy
78:37.in_short: These verses close Surah al-Naba' by describing the Day of Judgement as a scene of total silence before God, the Lord of everything, where none may speak except by His permission and only to say what is true. The Day is certain, and whoever wishes may still choose a path back to his Lord.

claims.text: Reciters differ on the grammatical case of 'Lord' (Rabb) and 'the Merciful' (al-Raḥmān) in this verse, whether read as a fresh sentence or as a continuation describing 'your Lord' from the previous verse. Commentators note both readings are valid.

sources.original_excerpt: واختلف القرّاء في قراءة ذلك
قرأ أهل الحجاز، وأبو عمرو: رب رفع
قرأ ابن مسعود ونافع... بالرفع

claims.text: The phrase 'they have no power to address Him' means that no created being can speak to God on that Day, or ask Him anything, except with His permission.

sources.original_excerpt: لا يقدر أحد من خلقه خطابه يوم القيامة، إلا من أذن له
لا يقدر الخلق على أن يكلموا الرب إلا بإذنه
لا يملكون أن يسألوه إلا فيما أذن لهم فيه
no one is able to begin addressing Him except by His permission
لا يقدر أحد منهم أن يخاطبه إلا بإذنه
لا يملكون أن يسألوه إلا فيما أذن لهم فيه

claims.text: A narrower reading takes 'address' specifically as intercession: none can intercede with God at all except by His leave.

sources.original_excerpt: وقال الكلبي: لا يملكون شفاعة إلا بإذنه
وقال الكسائي: لا يملكون منه خطابا بالشفاعة إلا بإذنه

claims.text: Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) notes the sentence can be read two ways: connected to the previous verse it means no one may question why one reward differs from another; read on its own it means no one in the Plain of Gathering can speak to God without permission, which will be granted in some stations of that Day but not in others.

sources.original_excerpt: no one dare speak about the grade... This permission will be granted in some of the positions of Gathering, and not in others.

claims.text: It has also been said the verse addresses the disbelievers specifically, who have no power to speak at all, while believers may intercede once given permission, as other verses about intercession by leave state.

sources.original_excerpt: وقيل: أراد الكفار لا يملكون منه خطابا، فأما المؤمنون فيشفعون

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads 'the Merciful' here as governing both reward and punishment together: it is itself an act of mercy that the defiant are punished, since justice requires that good and evil not be treated as equal.

sources.original_excerpt: یہ عین رحمت ہے کہ شر کو سزا ملے اور خیروشر برابر نہ ہوں ورنہ یہ تو ظلم ہوگا

claims.text: Commentators record several different explanations of who or what 'al-Rūḥ' is on that Day: a single mighty angel greater than the heavens, mountains, and all other angels (from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās); the angel Jibrīl (al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Saʿīd b. Jubayr); a created army in human form, with heads, hands and feet, that eats food, being neither angels nor men (Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and a hadith reported from Ibn ʿAbbās); mankind itself, the descendants of Adam (al-Ḥasan, Qatādah — with a note that Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly used to keep this view quiet); the souls of mankind standing between the two trumpet-blasts before returning to their bodies (ʿAṭiyyah, from Ibn ʿAbbās); and the Qur'an itself (Zayd b. Aslam, citing another verse that calls revelation 'a spirit/rūḥ').

sources.original_excerpt: اختلف أهل العلم في معنى الروح في هذا الموضع
واختلفوا في هذا الروح
واختلف في الروح على أقوال ثمانية
The word Ruh here is referring to the angel Jibril... Muqatil bin Hayyan said, 'The Ruh is the noblest of the angels'
يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ وهو جبريل عليه السلام، الذي هو أشرف الملائكة

Ruh (Spirit), according to some of the commentators, refers to the angel Jibra'il... According to certain Prophetic traditions, Ruh is not an angel but a huge army of Allah. They have heads, hands and legs.
شه‌ش ته‌فسیری بۆی هێناوه‌

claims.text: Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) states that identifying al-Rūḥ with Jibrīl is the preferred (rājiḥ) view, because the Qur'an elsewhere describes him as 'al-Rūḥ al-Amīn' who brings down revelation.

sources.original_excerpt: وكون المراد بالروح: جبريل - عليه السلام - هو الرأى الراجح

claims.text: Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) concludes that al-Rūḥ is indeed one of God's creations, but since no clear proof from the Qur'an or the Prophet ﷺ settles which of these views is meant, the correct position is to leave the matter open; not knowing exactly which is intended does no harm.

sources.original_excerpt: ولا خبر بشيء من ذلك أنه المعنيّ به دون غيره يجب التسليم له، ولاحجة تدلّ عليه، وغير ضائر الجهل به

claims.text: The Bengali commentary Ahsanul Bayaan reports that Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) regarded the view that al-Rūḥ means mankind (the descendants of Adam) as closer to being correct.

sources.original_excerpt: ইমাম ইবনে কাসীর আদম-সন্তান (মানুষ)-এর অর্থকেই সঠিকতার অধিক কাছাকাছি বলে মন্তব্য করেছেন

claims.text: Al-Shaʿbī explained that on that Day there will be two ranks (simāṭān) standing before the Lord of the Worlds: one rank of al-Rūḥ, and one rank of the angels.

sources.original_excerpt: هما سِمَاطان لربّ العالمين يوم القيامة
هما سماطا رب العالمين
there will be two rows. One row will be that of Ruh and the other will be that of the angels

claims.text: That none may speak except by permission on that Day is compared to other Qur'anic statements, such as 'who can intercede with Him except by His permission' and 'on the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His leave.'

sources.original_excerpt: This is as Allah says, مَن ذَا الَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُ إِلاَّ بِإِذْنِهِ

claims.text: A hadith is cited stating that on that Day none will speak except the Messengers, reported from Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه.

sources.original_excerpt: وَلَا يَتَكَلَّمُ يَوْمَئِذٍ إِلَّا الرُّسُل
رواه البخاري (٨٠٦) ومسلم (١٨٢)

report.graded_by: agreed upon by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, per the citation in the sources

claims.text: 'Said what is right' (qāla ṣawāban) is explained by some as simply speaking the truth, in this life or on that Day, and by others more specifically as the testimony 'there is no god but God' (lā ilāha illā Allāh), described as the furthest limit of what is right.

sources.original_excerpt: حقا في الدنيا وعمل به... لا إله إلا الله
في الدنيا، أي حقا. وقيل: قال: لا إله إلا الله
حقا؛ قاله الضحاك ومجاهد. وقال أبو صالح: لا إله إلا الله
and from the truth is the fact that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah

claims.text: One report holds that intercession will only be granted for someone who testified 'there is no god but God' in this world.

sources.original_excerpt: يشفعون لمن قال لا إله إلا الله

claims.text: One narration from ʿIkrimah describes when permission to speak is given: angels are asked where they are taking a group, and answer 'to the Fire' or 'to the Garden', explaining the reason, and are given leave to speak at that point.

sources.original_excerpt: يُمرّ بأناس من أهل النار على ملائكة، فيقولون: أين تذهبون بهؤلاء؟

claims.text: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that al-Rūḥ will declare on that Day: no one enters Paradise except by mercy, and no one enters the Fire except by his own deeds.

sources.original_excerpt: إن الروح يقول يوم القيامة: لا يدخل أحد الجنة إلا بالرحمة، ولا النار إلا بالعمل

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the silence of Jibrīl and the great angels standing in ranks as conveying overwhelming awe, fear, and majesty, an atmosphere heavier because even the sinless and the leading angels dare not speak.

sources.original_excerpt: جبرائیل (علیہ السلام) اور دوسرے سربرآور دو فرشتے بھی صف بستہ خاموش کھڑے ہوں گے

claims.text: 'That is the Day of Truth' means it is a certain, unavoidable occurrence, with no doubt about it, as affirmed by parallel statements elsewhere in the Qur'an about the inevitability of the Hour.

sources.original_excerpt: إنه حقّ كائن لا شكّ فيه
الكائن الواقع
أي الكائن الواقع
meaning, it will come to pass and there is no avoiding it
لا شك فى حدوثه، ولا ريب فى ثبوته
قیامت کا دن ایک اٹل حقیقت ہے

claims.text: 'Whoever wishes' means whoever wills may take, through obedience and righteous deeds, a path or return to his Lord, a way that brings him near before that Day arrives.

sources.original_excerpt: اتخذوا إلى الله مآبًا بطاعته، وما يقرّبهم إليه
فمن شاء رجع إلى الله بطاعته
مرجعا بالعمل الصالح
أي: عملا، وقدم صدق يرجع إليه يوم القيامة
فليتخذ إلى ربه مرجعًا بالعمل الصالح
ئه‌گه‌ڕێته‌وه‌ بۆ لای خوای گه‌وره‌ به‌ ته‌وبه‌كردن و به‌ كرده‌وه‌ی چاك

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī connects this to a saying attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, 'all good is by Your hand, and evil is not attributed to You,' noting that when a person does good it is referred back to God, and when he does evil it is counted against himself.

sources.original_excerpt: والخير كله بيديك، والشر ليس إليك

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads this verse as a sharp jolt aimed at those who doubted the Day and raised sceptical questions about it, urging them to use the time of respite still available before the Fire lies in ambush for them.

sources.original_excerpt: لوگو! ابھی فرصت کے اوقات موجود ہیں، مہلت ملی ہوئی ہے۔ اس سے فائدہ اٹھاﺅ

claims.text: Wahiduddin Khan draws an analogy from nature: every year calm weather is followed by rainstorms that bring desolate land back to green life, symbolically showing that the Hereafter emerging from the present world is just as possible as lush growth emerging from barren land.

sources.original_excerpt: the emergence of lush green foliage from dry barren land

78:37.essay_html:
These three verses close the surah with a single scene. God, described as Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, and as al-Raḥmān (the Merciful), presides over a Day when no creature can address Him without permission.1,2,3,4,9,13 Some readers narrow this to intercession specifically: no one may plead for another except by God's leave.2,3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) notes the line can also be read as tied to the previous verse, meaning no one may question why one person's reward differs from another's, with permission to speak granted at some points in the Gathering and withheld at others.7 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) also records that some took the silence as directed at the disbelievers, while believers may still intercede once given leave.3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads al-Raḥmān here as covering both reward and punishment, since justice itself, treating good and evil differently, is an expression of mercy.6

Verse 38 names two groups standing in that scene: al-Rūḥ and the angels. Commentators record several explanations of al-Rūḥ: a single mighty angel greater than the heavens and mountains, the angel Jibrīl, a created army in human shape with hands and feet who eat food, mankind itself, the souls of people between the two trumpet-blasts, or even the Qur'an.1,2,3,4,5,7,11,12,14 Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) prefers the Jibrīl reading, since the Qur'an elsewhere calls him 'the trustworthy spirit'.9 Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923), by contrast, declines to settle the question, holding that without clear proof it does no harm to leave it open.1 Ahsanul Bayaan reports that Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) leaned toward al-Rūḥ meaning mankind.12 Al-Shaʿbī pictured two ranks standing before the Lord of the Worlds, one of al-Rūḥ and one of the angels.1,2,3,7

The rule of speech only by permission echoes other verses: 'who can intercede with Him except by His leave' and 'no soul will speak except by His leave'.1,4,9 A hadith reported from Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه states that on that Day none speaks except the Messengers.4,14 When speech is permitted, it must be 'right' (ṣawāban): some take this as truth in general, others as specifically the testimony 'there is no god but God'.1,2,3,4 One report ties intercession to having spoken that testimony in this life.3,12 Another, from ʿIkrimah, pictures angels being asked where they are taking a group and answering 'to the Fire' or 'to the Garden', with leave to speak granted then.1 Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that al-Rūḥ will declare that no one enters Paradise except by mercy, and no one enters the Fire except by his own deeds.3 Sayyid Quṭb reads the silence of Jibrīl and the great angels as conveying the sheer weight of awe on that Day.6

Verse 39 names the Day 'true' (al-ḥaqq), a certain and unavoidable occurrence.1,2,3,4,8,9,11,12,14 Because of that certainty, whoever wills may take, through obedience and good deeds, a path back to his Lord, before that Day comes.1,2,3,5,13 Al-Qurṭubī links this to a saying that all good is referred back to God while evil is counted against the one who does it.3 Sayyid Quṭb reads the verse as a sharp jolt to shake those still in doubt, an urging to use the respite left before the Fire lies in ambush.6 Wahiduddin Khan points to the yearly return of green life to barren land as a natural sign that the return of life after death is no less possible.10

The commentators differ over the exact identity of al-Rūḥ and the precise sense of a few words, but they converge on the picture itself: a Day so charged with the Lord's majesty that even the greatest of creation stand silent, save by leave, and a door still open now for whoever wishes to walk back to Him.1,3,5,6,9,13

78:40.title: The Disbeliever's Wish for Dust
78:40.in_short: The surah closes with a warning: the reckoning is near, and on that Day every person will see what their own hands sent ahead. The disbeliever, faced with this, will cry out wishing he had simply been reduced to dust.

claims.text: The 'near torment' refers to the Day of Judgement or Resurrection. It is called 'near' because everything that is certainly coming counts as near, however far off it seems.

sources.original_excerpt: عذابًا قد دنا منكم وقرُب
يعني العذاب في الآخرة، وكل ما هو آت قريب
لأنه قد أزف مقبلا، وكل ما هو آت فهو قريب
هناك عذابا قريبا، سيحل بمن يستحقه عما قريب
عذاب يوم الآخرة القريب

claims.text: Some held that the 'near torment' means a punishment in this world rather than the next: Qatādah took it as worldly punishment (the nearer of the two possible torments), and Muqātil specified it as the killing of the Quraysh at Badr. Qurṭubī relays both but says the clearer view is that it concerns the Hereafter or death.

sources.original_excerpt: قال قتادة: عقوبة الدنيا... قال مقاتل: هي قتل قريش ببدر. والأظهر أنه عذاب الآخرة

claims.text: Qurṭubī reasons that the 'near torment' could mean death itself, since whoever dies has, in effect, begun his resurrection: he sees his place at once, whether it is Paradise or disgrace and torment.

sources.original_excerpt: هو الموت والقيامة؛ لأن من مات فقد قامت قيامته

claims.text: Mufti Muhammad Shafi, relaying al-Mazharī, notes a third possibility: 'day' here may mean the day of death, and 'will see' may mean seeing one's deeds in the grave or the intermediate state (barzakh), alongside the more common readings that the ledger of deeds is handed over or that deeds appear bodily on the Plain of Gathering.

On that Day every person will see what his hands sent forth: every deed, good and bad, old and new, will be presented before him, echoed by verses describing people finding their deeds 'present' before them and being told of what they sent ahead.

sources.original_excerpt: كل امرئ يرى في ذلك اليوم ما قدم من العمل مثبتا في صحيفته

claims.text: Al-Ḥasan read 'the man' (al-marʾ) here specifically as the believer, the one who dreads both minor and major sin, and so finds his own deeds when he looks.

sources.original_excerpt: المرء المؤمن يحذَر الصغيرة، ويخاف الكبيرة
المرء هاهنا المؤمن في قول الحسن

claims.text: Qurṭubī supports the believer-reading contextually: since Allah then says separately 'and the disbeliever will say...', this shows the earlier 'the man' must mean the believer, the disbeliever's case being stated apart.

sources.original_excerpt: ولما قال: ويقول الكافر علم أنه أراد بالمرء المؤمن

claims.text: Some named the specific people meant: 'the man' as Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, and 'the disbeliever' as Abū Jahl. Muqātil said the first phrase was revealed about Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, and the second about his brother al-Aswad.

sources.original_excerpt: المرء هاهنا: أبي بن خلف وعقبة بن أبي معيط

claims.text: Others held that 'the man' is general, meaning every human being who will see the reward for what he earned, without restricting it to any one person.

sources.original_excerpt: وقيل: هو عام في كل أحد وإنسان

claims.text: A widely reported narrative explains the disbeliever's wish: on Judgement Day the earth will be spread flat like a hide, and all animals gathered. Retribution will be settled between them, even a hornless sheep being avenged against one that gored it with horns. When this is finished, the animals will be commanded, 'Be dust,' and they will become dust. Seeing this, the disbeliever will cry, 'Would that I were dust!' — wishing he too could escape reckoning by simply ceasing to be.

sources.original_excerpt: قال لها: كوني ترابا، قال: فعند ذلك يقول الكافر: يا ليتني كنت ترابًا
كوني ترابا، فعند ذلك يقول الكافر: يا ليتني كنت ترابا
قيل لها: كوني ترابا، فعند ذلك يقول الكافر: يا ليتني كنت ترابا

report.graded_by: reports from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar, left ungraded by these sources; source [11] cites it via al-Mustadrak, Musnad Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh and al-Silsilah al-Ṣaḥīḥah

claims.text: Another identification takes 'the disbeliever' here as Iblīs himself. He had mocked Adam عليه السلام for being made from dust while boasting his own creation from fire. On the Day, seeing Adam's descendants rewarded, he wishes he were dust — that is, wishes he were in Adam's place. One report even has the dust itself answer him, 'No, and no honour for you either — who made you like me?'

sources.original_excerpt: إن الكافر هاهنا إبليس وذلك أنه عاب آدم وأنه خلق من التراب وافتخر بأنه خلق من النار
الكافر: هاهنا إبليس وذلك أنه عاب آدم بأنه خلق من تراب

claims.text: A further reading holds that believing jinn, like the animals, will be commanded 'Return to dust,' and the disbeliever, seeing them so reduced, wishes he were dust as they are.

sources.original_excerpt: عُودُوا ترابًا، فإذا نظر الكفار إليهم قد عادوا ترابًا
عودوا ترابا فيعودون ترابا
قيل لسائر الأمم ولمؤمني الجن: عودوا ترابا، فيعودون ترابا

claims.text: Qurṭubī states the more correct view, held by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Zuhrī, al-Kalbī and Mujāhid, is that believing jinn do not become dust but dwell in courtyards around Paradise, since they are morally accountable like human beings, rewarded and punished.

sources.original_excerpt: وهذا أصح... مؤمنو الجنة حول الجنة في ربض ورحاب وليسوا فيها

claims.text: Some read the wish differently: 'would that I were dust' means 'would that I had never been raised at all,' comparable to the despairing cry elsewhere, 'would that I had not been given my record.'

sources.original_excerpt: أي لم أبعث، كما قال: يا ليتني لم أوت كتابيه

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr sums up that the disbeliever will simply wish he had never existed at all in this world, having seen Allah's punishment and his own wicked deeds written against him by the noble recording angels.

Al-Saʿdī reads the verse as a call to look now, in this life, at what one sends ahead, paralleling the Qurʾanic call elsewhere to let every soul look at what it has sent forward for tomorrow. Whoever finds good should thank Allah; whoever finds otherwise should blame only himself. This, he says, is why the disbelievers will wish for death, out of the sheer severity of their regret.

sources.original_excerpt: فإن وجد خيرا فليحمد الله، وإن وجد غير ذلك فلا يلومن إلا نفسه

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the disbeliever's cry as a mark of total despair: he would rather cease to exist entirely, be reduced to nothing, than face that punishment. Quṭb links this stance to those who, in the present, raise doubting questions about the reality of this Day.

Isrār Aḥmad stresses how near the punishment truly is, since death itself may come at any moment, citing the Prophet's ﷺ saying that the grave is either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire. He reads the disbeliever's wish as a wish that he had never been honoured with being human at all.

sources.original_excerpt: اِنَّمَا الْقَبْرُ رَوْضَۃٌ مِنْ رِیَاضِ الْجَنَّۃِ اَوْ حُفْرَۃٌ مِنْ حُفَرِ النَّارِ

report.graded_by: hadith cited by source 8 without grading

claims.text: Ṭanṭāwī reads the verse as cutting off, in the most eloquent way, every excuse of the excuse-makers, before a Day comes when neither wealth nor children will avail anyone except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.

sources.original_excerpt: قطع أعذار المعتذرين بأبلغ وجه

claims.text: Wahīduddīn Khān draws a natural analogy: the yearly pattern of calm weather followed by storms and rain that turn desolate land into flourishing greenery is a sign, in symbolic fashion, of how the Hereafter's emergence from the present world is equally possible.

78:40.essay_html:
The surah closes with a warning that the torment is near 1,2,4,5,9,13. It is called near, the commentators explain, simply because anything certain to come counts as near, however far off it feels 2,5. Some read this differently: Qatādah took the near torment as a worldly punishment, and Muqātil specified it as the killing of the Quraysh at Badr, though Qurṭubī (d. 1273) says the clearer reading points to the Hereafter 3. Qurṭubī himself suggests it may mean death, since whoever dies has, in effect, begun his own resurrection, seeing his place at once 3. Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, relaying al-Mazharī, adds a further possibility: the 'day' may be the day of death, and the seeing may happen in the grave, the barzakh 7.

On that Day, every person sees what his hands sent forth: every deed, good and bad, old and new, laid out before him 1,2,4,7,9,13,14. Al-Ḥasan read 'the man' here as specifically the believer, the one who dreads even small sin and fears the great, and so finds his own record when he looks 1,3. Qurṭubī supports this from the shape of the verse itself: since Allah goes on to say separately 'and the disbeliever will say', the earlier 'the man' must be the believer, the disbeliever's case stated apart 3. Others named specific people, Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ as 'the man', Abū Jahl as 'the disbeliever' 3, while still others took the words as general, meaning every human being who sees the reward of what he earned 3.

A widely carried narrative explains the disbeliever's wish. On Judgement Day, the earth is spread flat, and every animal is gathered. Old wrongs between them are settled, even a hornless sheep avenged against one that gored it. When this is done, the animals are told, 'Be dust,' and they become dust 1,2,3,4,7,11,12,14. Watching this, the disbeliever cries out that he too wishes he were dust, wishing he could simply cease to be rather than face his reckoning. Some further identify 'the disbeliever' here as Iblīs, who had mocked Adam عليه السلام for being made of dust while boasting his own creation from fire. Seeing Adam's descendants rewarded, he now wishes he were dust himself, in Adam's place, one report even having the dust answer him back: no honour for him either 2,3. A related strand holds that believing jinn, like the animals, will be told to return to dust, and the disbeliever wishes he were among them 1,2,3. Qurṭubī, however, judges the more correct view, held by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Zuhrī, al-Kalbī and Mujāhid, to be that believing jinn dwell instead in courtyards around Paradise, since they are morally accountable exactly as human beings are 3.

The wish itself is also read another way: 'would that I were dust' may simply mean 'would that I had never been raised at all', matching the despair voiced elsewhere over an unwanted record of deeds 3. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) sums the moment up plainly: having seen the punishment and his own wicked deeds written against him by the recording angels, the disbeliever wishes he had simply never existed 4.

Several commentators draw out what this means for the reader now. Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) reads the verse as a call to examine, in this life, what one is sending ahead, paralleling the Qurʾanic call for every soul to look at what it sends forward for tomorrow; whoever finds good should thank Allah, whoever finds otherwise has only himself to blame, and this, he says, is the root of the disbeliever's wish for death 5. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the same cry as total despair, a preference for total non-existence over facing that punishment, and ties it to those who today raise doubting questions about this reality 6. Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) stresses instead how near death itself always is, citing the Prophet's ﷺ saying that the grave is either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire, and reads the disbeliever's wish as regret at ever having been given the honour of being human 8. Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) reads the whole verse as cutting off, in the most eloquent way, every excuse anyone might offer, before a Day when neither wealth nor children help anyone except the one who comes with a sound heart 9.

Wahīduddīn Khān (d. 2021) points to a natural pattern as a quiet sign of the same truth: the yearly return of storms and rain that turn barren land green again shows, in symbolic form, that the world's rebirth into a Hereafter is no less possible 10.

The surah ends here on this single image: a person facing his own deeds, and a disbeliever so undone by what he sees that he would rather be dust than himself.

78:17.essay_html:
The Day of Decision (yawm al-faṣl) is the Day of Judgement, a fixed appointment set by Allah for reward and punishment, covering the first and the last generations.1,2,3,4,7,9,13 It carries that name because on it Allah separates and judges between His creatures according to their deeds.1,3,9 Mīqāt, the appointed time, is a set time for an action. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) notes its timing cannot be brought forward or delayed, and no one knows it except Allah.4,9

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads this verse against the ordered pattern of life just described and the ordered pattern of the universe itself. Both point any thoughtful person to the same conclusion: man is not left without account.6 Wahīd al-Dīn Khān (d. 2021) makes a related point. A world with a beginning like this one must have a fitting end.10 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) ties the verse to the blessings listed earlier in the surah. Responsibility travels with privilege, so a day of reckoning had to be fixed.8

The Trumpet (al-Ṣūr) is described in one report as a horn.1 Qatāda is recorded reading al-Ṣūr here as meaning 'creation' itself.1 People then come 'in crowds' (afwājan), meaning troop after troop.1,2,3,4,9,13 al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) explains this as each nation coming with the messenger sent to it, comparing it to 'the Day We call every people with their leader' (17:71).1,3,4,13,14

A hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه, has the Prophet ﷺ say that 'forty' lies between the two blowings of the Trumpet, without saying whether days, months or years are meant. Then rain falls from the sky and bodies sprout as plants do. Every part of a person decays except the tailbone, from which the body is reassembled.4 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) relays a further report, from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī رضي الله عنه, that people will come to the Gathering in three groups: one full-fed and mounted, one barefoot, one dragged on its faces, with other narrations speaking of ten groups reconciled as different sortings by deed.7 al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) relays a longer report tied to Muʿādh ibn Jabal رضي الله عنه, in which the Prophet ﷺ wept before describing ten kinds of people raised in altered forms matching their sins in life, from gossips as apes to corrupt judges made blind.3 Neither of these two reports carries a stated grading in the source.

Quṭb cautions that only the Trumpet's name is given, and that it will sound. Pressing further adds nothing, since Allah has given what knowledge is needed. He pictures people pouring from their graves like ants, an assembly beyond anything seen before, its very scale producing dread.6 Isrār Aḥmad likens the scene to 70:43, where people are described rushing from their graves 'as if racing toward a target-post.'8 Khān adds that arrogance feels pleasant in this world because it satisfies the ego, but in the Hereafter, once the ego shows its true shape, what once felt delightful becomes torment.10

The sky then opens into what look like gates. Reciters differ on the verb: the Kufan reading is lighter, others read it intensified, meaning the sky is torn open.2 Commentators take this as the sky splitting into paths for the angels to descend.1,2,3,4,9,11,12,13,14 al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī also record another reading: the sky breaks into pieces like the cut wood-panels used for doors, with 'gates' standing in for 'like gates,' the word 'like' dropped, much as one says 'so-and-so is a lion' meaning 'like a lion.'1,3 A further reading takes 'it became gates' to mean the sky comes to possess gates, since it turns wholly into openings.2,3 al-Qurṭubī relays a saying that every person has two gates in heaven, one for deeds and one for provision, opening when the Hour comes, and he notes the hadith of the Night Journey, where Jibrīl عليه السلام sought a gate's opening before it was granted.3 Neither report is graded in the source.

The mountains, taken as the world's picture of firmness, are set in motion and reduced to a mirage, something that looks present but is not there.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,14 Ibn Kathīr draws this together with other Qur'anic descriptions of the mountains' end: passing like clouds (27:88), turning to carded wool (101:5), blasted into dust leaving a level plain (20:105-107), and the earth appearing levelled (18:47).4,12 Sarāb, mirage, is glossed as the illusion of open land, where something looks like water from afar but vanishes on approach.3,7,9,12 al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) adds that this is also when Allah decides between His creatures by a judgement that wrongs no one.5 Quṭb pictures a scene beyond full human imagination: the mountains shatter into particles scattered in the air, and these particles catch the light the way a mirage does, making the eye see what is not there.6

A fixed appointment, a trumpet, a crowd without number, a sky turned to gates, mountains turned to mirage: the commentators read each of these as a mark set down for a Day already decided.

78:31.essay_html:
After describing the fate of those who denied the Day, the passage turns to the mutaqqūn, those mindful of God, and this is placed deliberately as a contrast with what came before7,8,9. Mafāzan names the winning they gain: the classical reports trace it to relief from the Fire into Paradise, attaining what was sought1,2,3,4,9,13. Some early voices glossed it more simply as a pleasant place of recreation, and Ibn Kathīr judged this reading closer to the mark, given what follows1,2,4. Sayyid Quṭb pictures the scene sharply: the Fire had lain in wait like a hunter for its prey; here are those who slipped free of it, arriving at the place of triumph6.

That triumph is spelled out in images. There are ḥadāʾiq, walled gardens holding palm trees, vines, and other trees1,3,9, and grapevines named specifically for their standing and abundance among fruits1,5,9. Quṭb adds that grapes are singled out because the first hearers of the Qur'an knew and prized them well6.

There are companions too: kawāʿib, young women in the fullness of youth, and atrāb, matched in age with one another1,2,3,4,9,11,12,14. Al-Saʿdī puts that age at thirty-three, the most balanced point of youth, and notes it is the way of age-mates to be close and sociable together5. A footnote in one modern tafsīr allows the phrase to mean simply that the companions match one another in age11.

A cup, kaʾsan dihāqan, is offered, and the word dihāq carries three readings among the commentators: brimming full1,2,3,4, coming one after another without pause1,2,3, or clear and pure1,2,3. Al-Ṭabarī traces the root to al-dahq, a firm continuous pressing, so the cup stays pressed full for its drinker1. Al-Qurṭubī records a further derivation, tracing dihāq to the boards used for pressing, so the wine is described as pressed and clarified3.

In that gathering they hear no laghw, idle talk, and no kidhdhāb, lying against one another1,2,3,4,5,9,13. Al-Qurṭubī reasons that, unlike the people of this world, the drink of Paradise does not cloud the mind, so no vain word follows it3. Ibn Kathīr links the phrase to a matching description in Sūrat al-Ṭūr, "free of vain talk and free of sin"4. Quṭb adds that lying elsewhere breeds argument, while in Paradise the truth is plain and there is nothing left to dispute6. The reciters differ on how كِذَّابًا is pronounced: al-Kisāʾī read it lightened, against the majority's doubled form, which al-Ṭabarī preferred as the reading of the wider body of reciters1,3. Wahīd al-Dīn Khān reads the scene as reserved for those who, in this life, kept themselves from vanity and falsehood10.

The passage closes by naming this jazāʾan, a reward, and also ʿaṭāʾan, a gift. Al-Ṭabarī and Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ read the pairing together: what is given answers to deeds, yet exceeds them, since no deed alone could earn Paradise; it is granted by God's favour1,7. Shafīʿ cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said no one enters Paradise by deeds alone except through God's grace, and that this held even for him ﷺ when the Companions asked7. Ḥisāban is read two ways: sufficient and abundant, from the Arabic idiom of giving someone enough that he says, "that is enough for me"2,3,4,9; or measured exactly against their deeds, multiplied tenfold or up to seven-hundredfold as promised elsewhere in the Qur'an1,3. One modern tafsīr notes the asymmetry: punishment is measured exactly to the offence, while the reward given here exceeds what is strictly owed11. Isrār Aḥmad reads the whole as recompense for their labour and sacrifice8, and a report relayed by Shafīʿ illustrates how sincerity outweighs scale: a Companion's small gift for God's sake was said to outweigh a mountain given by someone after them7. Quṭb notes the sound of the passage itself, the rhyme between jazāʾ and ʿaṭāʾ, closing the scenes of the Day with which the sūrah has been concerned6.

What is promised to the mindful is named twice, as jazāʾ and as ʿaṭāʾ, reward and gift together, because, as the commentators read it, what is given answers their deeds and still outruns them, sufficient until, as the old idiom has it, one can only say: enough.

78:6.title: Signs in Earth and Sky
78:6.in_short: This passage lists a string of ordinary but wondrous realities — the earth, mountains, human pairing, sleep, night and day, the seven heavens, the sun, and the rain that grows food and gardens — as proof that the God who arranged all this can also bring about the resurrection the surah's opening describes.

claims.text: The whole list of created things in these verses functions as proof of Allah's power to raise the dead: the One able to bring these things into being is able to bring people back to life.
Mihad means a spread or bed, likened to the cradle prepared for a child to sleep on.

original_terms.gloss: a prepared spread or bed, like a cradle

claims.text: Sayyid Qutb reads mihad as combining two close senses: made ready for travelling about, and soft like a cradle. He says the earth's fitness for human life is a plain fact any person can grasp, and one that deepens the more human knowledge advances.
Al-Baghawi notes that this recounting of God's works aims to make people recognise His oneness.
The mountains are described as pegs (awtad) driven into the earth to stop it shaking or swaying with its inhabitants.

Sayyid Qutb says the Quran only alludes briefly to how mountains stabilise the earth, and leaves the mechanism open: perhaps balancing sea depths against mountain heights, easing tension between the earth's inner and outer layers, or checking earthquakes and volcanic activity at sensitive points. He notes the Quran often points to realities that people confirm only centuries later.
A footnote observes that a mountain's roots, driven into the ground like pegs, run far deeper than its visible height, some ten to fifteen times as long.
Being created in pairs (azwaj) means male and female, so that procreation continues and the human race is preserved.

Some commentators take azwaj more broadly, as varieties or kinds: differing in stature, colour, and looks, so that people are tested through these differences, the favoured giving thanks and the less-favoured showing patience.
Ibn Kathir links this pairing to 30:21: it brings affection and mercy between the pair and is the means by which procreation happens.

Sayyid Qutb reflects that the difference of male and female is fixed at the level of the seed itself, though the seed carries no visible mark of sex. Only Allah directs a given seed toward becoming male or female.

Commentators dispute the root of subat (the word used for sleep as rest). Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923 CE) ties it to sukūn, stillness, the same root that names Saturday (yawm al-sabt) as a day of rest for the Children of Israel. Al-Baghawī cites al-Zajjāj: a cutting-off of movement and breath. Others take subāt from a root meaning 'to cut off', so that sleep cuts off one's daily business. Al-Qurṭubī surveys several derivations (rest, the loosening of hair, cutting, ease of travel) and notes that Ibn al-Anbārī rejected 'rest' as a valid sense for subāt altogether.
Sleep is granted as rest and stillness for the body, resembling death though the soul has not left it.

Sayyid Qutb reflects at length on sleep: it suspends perception and action for a while, in a state that is neither death nor full life, and restores exhausted nerves and body. He calls this a mystery known only to its Creator, needed by every living thing, and compares it to the calming drowsiness (nu'ās) Allah sent on believers at Badr and Uḥud.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976 CE) notes sleep is given equally, indeed most readily, to the poor and labouring class, regardless of comfortable beds or lack of them, and is imposed by Allah's mercy even on someone who wishes to stay awake.
The night is a covering: its darkness wraps and conceals people the way a garment covers the one who wears it.
Some read night here simply as stillness (sakan) granted to people, reported from Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī, and Qatādah.
The day is made for livelihood: its light lets people move about seeking their sustenance and Allah's bounty.
Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ observes that night and day complete one another: without daylight for earning a living, sleep would simply turn into death.
The seven heavens are built firmly overhead, with no cracks or flaws, and they endure unbroken through time.
Al-Ṭabarī notes that the Arabs called a house's roof a 'building' (bina'), and since the sky serves as earth's roof, the Quran speaks to them in their own idiom by calling the heavens 'built'.
A footnote cites a distance of five hundred years' travel between each of the seven heavens as evidence of their firmness.

Sayyid Qutb suggests the 'seven strong' heavens might refer to seven vast galactic clusters, while stating the true referent is known only to Allah, and that human knowledge of the cosmos, however impressive it looks, remains very limited.
The 'blazing lamp' (sirāj wahhāj) is the sun, described as radiant and luminous.
Al-Saʿdī and Muqātil note that the word wahhāj joins both meanings of the sun's benefit: its light, which creation cannot do without, and its heat, source of further benefits.
Sayyid Qutb connects the sun's heat to the water cycle: it warms the seas and lifts the clouds that later pour down as rain.

Commentators dispute what al-muʿṣirāt (the source of the rain) means. One view: winds that press or wring the rain out of clouds. Another: rain-laden clouds that have not yet released their rain, likened to a woman nearing her monthly cycle (muʿṣir) before it begins. A third, called 'strange' by al-Ṭabarī and Ṭanṭāwī: the heavens themselves. Al-Ṭabarī states the 'clouds' reading is the soundest, based on the grammar of the preposition used (min rather than bi), a preference Ibn Kathīr also reports as favoured by Ibn Jarīr (al-Ṭabarī).

original_terms.gloss: the rain-laden clouds (or, on another reading, the winds that press rain from them)

claims.text: Thajjāj describes the rain as pouring forth continuously and copiously, one downpour following another.

As linguistic support for thajj meaning abundant, continuous flow, al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī cite a hadith describing the best of Hajj as 'al-ʿajj wa'l-thajj' (raising the voice in pilgrim's call, and the shedding of sacrificial blood), and Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith about a woman with prolonged bleeding using the same root to describe her profuse flow.

report.graded_by: not graded in the sources cited

claims.text: Ḥabb (grain) refers to what people store and eat, such as wheat and barley; nabāt (plants) refers to pasture and greenery eaten by grazing animals.
Jannāt alfāfā (luxuriant gardens) means gardens whose trees and branches are densely intertwined, growing close together.

Al-Ṭabarī notes an ellipsis in the phrase: literally 'and gardens', it is understood to mean 'and the fruit of gardens', with 'fruit' left out because the sense is clear from context. Grammarians also debated the singular form behind the plural alfāf (laff or lafīf).

78:6.essay_html:
This stretch of the surah answers disbelief in the resurrection with a list of ordinary wonders. If God can arrange the earth, the mountains, human beings, sleep, the sky, and the rain, the commentators note, He can certainly bring the dead back to life3,4,9,10. Al-Baghawī (d. 1122 CE) adds that recounting these works is meant to make people recognise God's oneness2.

The earth is called a mihād, a spread or bed, likened to a cradle prepared for a child1,2,3,9. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads mihād as carrying both 'made ready for travel' and 'soft like a cradle', and says the earth's fitness for human life is obvious at any level of knowledge, and only deepens as science advances6. The mountains are pegs (awtād), driven in to stop the earth shaking with its people1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14. Quṭb leaves the exact mechanism open, wondering whether mountains balance sea-depths against land-heights, ease tension in the earth's crust, or curb earthquakes at sensitive points, noting the Quran often points to things confirmed only centuries later6. One note adds that a mountain's buried root runs far deeper than its visible height12.

Being made in pairs (azwāj) means male and female, for procreation and the continuation of the race1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14, though some commentators also read azwāj as varieties of colour and stature by which people are tested1,3,9,12. Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373 CE) ties the pairing to verse 30:21, affection and mercy arising between the pair4. Quṭb goes further: the difference of sex is fixed already in the seed, which carries no visible mark of it, so that only God directs a given seed toward maleness or femaleness6.

Sleep as subāt draws a scatter of readings. Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923 CE) ties subāt to stillness, the same root behind Saturday as a day of rest for the Children of Israel1; al-Baghawī cites al-Zajjāj's 'cutting-off of movement and breath', and a competing view that it cuts off one's daily business2. Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) surveys several derivations, and records that Ibn al-Anbārī actually rejected 'rest' as a valid sense for the word at all3. Whatever the root, the commentators agree sleep is rest for the body, close to death though the soul has not left it4,5,11,12,13,14. Quṭb dwells on sleep as a state neither death nor full life, a mystery known only to its Creator, comparing it to the calming drowsiness sent on believers at Badr and Uḥud6. Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976 CE) observes that this gift reaches the poor and labouring class as readily as anyone, imposed by mercy even on those who wish to stay awake7. Night is called a covering, its darkness wrapping people the way a garment wraps its wearer, though some report it simply as stillness (sakan)1,2,3,4,9,11,13,14. Day is for livelihood, its light letting people move about and seek their sustenance1,2,3,4,9,11,13,14; Shafīʿ notes the two complete each other, since without daylight for earning, sleep would simply become death7.

The seven heavens overhead are described as firm, without cracks, enduring through time1,2,3,4,5,9,11,13,14. Al-Ṭabarī explains the Quran calls the sky 'built' because Arabs called a house's roof a building, and the sky is earth's roof, so the address matches their own idiom1. One note cites a five-hundred-year distance between each heaven as a mark of their firmness12. Quṭb wonders whether the 'seven strong' might be seven vast galactic clusters, while insisting the true referent is known only to God, and that human knowledge of the cosmos remains very limited however large it looks6. The 'blazing lamp' is the sun, described as radiant and luminous1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14; al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) notes the word wahhāj joins the sun's two gifts, light that creation cannot do without and heat that brings further benefits2,5. Quṭb links that heat to the water cycle, warming seas and lifting the clouds that later fall as rain6.

The source of the rain, al-muʿṣirāt, is disputed. Some take it as winds that press the rain from clouds; others, as rain-laden clouds not yet released, likened to a woman nearing her cycle (muʿṣir) before it starts; a third view, which al-Ṭabarī and Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010 CE) call strange, takes it as the heavens themselves. Al-Ṭabarī judges the 'clouds' reading soundest on grammatical grounds, a preference Ibn Kathīr reports as well1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,13. The word thajjāj describes the rain as pouring copiously and continuously1,2,3,4,11,12,13; as linguistic support, al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī cite a hadith calling the best of Hajj 'al-ʿajj wa'l-thajj' (raised voices and shed blood), and Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith about a woman's profuse bleeding using the same root, both left ungraded in these sources1,3,4.

From that rain come grain for people to eat and store, and pasture for grazing animals1,2,3,4,5,11,12,13,14, and gardens described as alfāf, densely intertwined1,2,3,4,5,11,12,13,14. Al-Ṭabarī notes the phrase literally says only 'gardens', with 'fruit of' understood and left out because the sense is plain1,3.

Each item in this list is something any person can see for themselves, earth underfoot, mountains on the horizon, sleep at day's end, rain out of cloud, and the commentators read it as an argument that needs no special learning: the God who arranged all this so exactly is not short of power to bring the dead back to life.

78:1.title: The Great News They Dispute
78:1.in_short: The surah opens on the buzz of dispute in Makka: what are they all asking about? It is the 'great news' - resurrection, and the Qur'an that announces it - over which people have split into believers and deniers. The answer given twice is blunt: they will find out.

claims.text: ʿAmma (عمّ) is a contraction of the preposition ʿan (about) and the interrogative mā (what); the nūn is assimilated into the mīm, and the alif of mā is dropped so the question form is distinguished from a statement.

original_terms.gloss: contraction of 'about what', from ʿan + mā

claims.text: The question is not asked to gather real information; it is a rhetorical form used to express astonishment and to magnify the seriousness of what follows.

A report traced to al-Ḥasan says that when the Prophet ﷺ was sent and began calling people to belief in his prophethood, to the truth of what he brought, and to resurrection, the Makkans started disputing the matter among themselves, and this verse came down about that dispute.

report.graded_by: not graded in the cited sources

claims.text: 'They' in 'they are asking' is understood from context to mean Quraysh (the Makkan polytheists), even though they are not named beforehand, because the setting makes clear who is meant.

One reading of 'the great news' (al-nabaʾ al-ʿaẓīm) takes it to mean the Qur'an itself, a view traced to Mujāhid and said by some to be held by the majority, supported by the parallel phrase 'say: it is a great news' (38:67).

original_terms.gloss: the momentous, weighty piece of news

claims.text: Another reading, traced to Qatādah, takes 'the great news' to mean the Resurrection itself; this is presented as the dominant view among the two readings.

A broader reading takes 'the great news' to cover the whole message the Prophet ﷺ brought together: that resurrection is real, that the Qur'an is from Allah, and that he is truthful in what he commands and forbids.

By not naming the news directly and only describing it as 'great', the verse builds suspense and magnifies the matter; this indirect approach is judged more forceful and more unsettling than a plain statement would have been.
People have split into two camps over this great news: those who affirm it and those who deny it.
Qatādah is reported to have noted that people all agreed on death itself, since they witness it, but differed specifically over resurrection after death.
A different account, traced to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, links the dispute to the Jews asking the Prophet ﷺ many questions, with Allah informing him of their disagreement.

The disagreement was not uniform: some flatly denied resurrection as inconceivable, others counted on their own gods to spare them from any reckoning, positions the Qur'an quotes elsewhere from such deniers.
Some scholars held that both believers and disbelievers were among those asking, but for opposite reasons: the believer asked to grow in fear and readiness, the disbeliever to mock.

A distinct reading holds that the Arabs were not deniers of an afterlife as such, but doubted the particular kind of Hereafter the Qur'an described, specifically doubting that rejecting Muhammad ﷺ would bring them humiliation there.
Kallā functions as a word of sharp rebuke and denial, rejecting the disputants' stance outright rather than merely disagreeing with it.

original_terms.gloss: a particle of firm rebuke and denial, roughly 'certainly not'

claims.text: 'They will come to know' is a threat that the truth of the matter will be forced on them, whether at death, on the Day of Judgement, or when punishment actually descends.
This is described as a severe threat and a direct warning against those who deny the Day of Judgement.

The object of 'they will know' is deliberately left unstated, which generalises the dread; they will know with certainty what awaits them, comparable to the Qur'an's remark elsewhere that what people see as distant, Allah sees as near.
Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to have said the first 'kallā sayaʿlamūn' addresses the disbelievers specifically.

report.graded_by: not graded by the cited sources

claims.text: The repetition of the same warning intensifies the threat; the second occurrence is judged stronger and more emphatic than the first, and is also described simply as 'warning upon warning'.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to have read the second 'kallā sayaʿlamūn' as addressed to the believers, and he is said to have recited it that way; al-Qurṭubī notes a reversed version of this attribution was also reported.

report.graded_by: not graded by the cited sources

claims.text: The common recitation reads both instances of 'they will know' in the third person, matching the earlier third-person verbs; al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Mālik ibn Dīnār are reported to have read both in the second person ('you will know') instead.

The veil between this world and the intermediate realm (barzakh) is death alone; the grave is the first stage of the barzakh, and the moment a person reaches it the reality is unveiled, so this knowledge is not far off for anyone.

original_terms.gloss: the intermediate realm between death and resurrection

claims.text: The physical order of the present world implies it must have a matching future: a great beginning demands a fitting great end, so this world is not going to finish without a befitting close.
After this double warning, the discourse is understood to turn toward evident signs in creation, offered as proof of Allah's power to bring about resurrection.

78:1.essay_html:
The surah opens mid-argument. ʿAmma yatasāʾalūn, "what are they asking about", is built from ʿan (about) and mā (what), fused together.1,2,3,7,9 But the question is not really seeking information. It is asked to express astonishment, to magnify how serious the matter is.2,6,9 A report traced to al-Ḥasan says that once the Prophet ﷺ began calling people to belief, to the Qur'an, and to resurrection, the Makkans fell into dispute among themselves, and this verse addresses that dispute.1,2,7,9,12 "They" is understood as Quraysh from the setting, even without being named.1,3,9

The thing they argue over is called "the great news" (al-nabaʾ al-ʿaẓīm). One reading, traced to Mujāhid and said to be held by the majority, takes it as the Qur'an itself, pointing to the parallel phrase elsewhere, "say: it is a great news" (38:67).1,2,3,11,14 Another reading, traced to Qatādah, takes it as the Resurrection, and this is presented as the stronger of the two readings.1,2,3,4,7,11,14 A broader reading folds both together: the great news is the whole package the Prophet ﷺ brought, that resurrection is real, that the Qur'an is from Allah, and that he is truthful.9,13 By naming it only as "great" rather than saying outright what it is, the verse builds suspense, and this indirect approach is judged more unsettling than a flat statement would have been.6,9

Over this news, people split into two camps: those who affirm it and those who deny it.1,2,3,4,9,13 Qatādah is reported to have observed that everyone agreed about death itself, since they see it happen, but differed specifically over resurrection after death.1,3 A separate account links the dispute instead to the Jews questioning the Prophet ﷺ, with Allah informing him of their disagreement.3 The objections themselves varied: some flatly called resurrection inconceivable, others trusted their own gods to spare them any reckoning, positions the Qur'an quotes from deniers elsewhere.8,11 Some held that both believers and disbelievers were asking, but for opposite reasons, the believer to grow in fear and readiness, the disbeliever to mock.9,12 A distinct reading, from Wahiduddin Khan, holds that the Arabs were not deniers of an afterlife altogether, but doubted the particular Hereafter the Qur'an described, especially that rejecting Muhammad ﷺ would bring them humiliation there.10

Kallā is a word of sharp rebuke, rejecting their stance outright rather than merely disputing it.1,2,3,6,9 "They will come to know" threatens that the truth will be forced on them, whether at death, at Judgement, or when punishment actually falls.1,4,5,7,8,9,13 Ibn Kathīr رحمه الله calls it a severe threat and a direct warning.4 What exactly they will come to know is left unstated, which widens the dread rather than narrowing it, echoed elsewhere in the Qur'an's remark that what people see as distant, Allah sees as near.9 Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to have said the first "kallā sayaʿlamūn" addresses the disbelievers specifically.1,2,3

The line is then repeated, and the repetition sharpens the blow: the second occurrence is judged stronger than the first, described also simply as "warning upon warning".2,3,4,7,9 Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to have read the second occurrence as addressed to the believers instead, though al-Qurṭubī رحمه الله notes a reversed version of this attribution was also reported.1,2,3 The standard recitation keeps both verbs in the third person, "they will know", matching the earlier verses, though al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Mālik ibn Dīnār are reported to have read both in the second person, "you will know".3 Isrār Aḥmad رحمه الله adds that the veil between this world and the barzakh, the realm between death and resurrection, is death alone, so the grave itself is the first stage where the reality becomes plain.8 Wahiduddin Khan notes that the physical order of the present world implies a matching future, a great beginning demanding a fitting end.10 The discourse then turns, as several sources note, toward the visible signs of creation, offered next as proof of the same power that can bring about resurrection.6,7

Whether named as the Qur'an or as the Resurrection, the great news is the same news the disputants could not settle by argument. The answer given to them, twice over, is not an argument at all: they will know.
